applogiq.problem: The public site and admin ran as two disconnected products. Marketing content, inbound leads, and internal data lived in different models — so applogiq.org could not operate as a real acquisition engine, and operators could not act on demand from one console.
approach: Rebuilt applogiq.org and the internal admin as two frontends on one shared data contract: Next.js for SEO and routing on the marketing site, a client-driven admin for operators.
Designed modular React + TypeScript + Tailwind UI so marketing pages, lead capture, and admin tables share one interaction language instead of two design systems.
Wired public-site lead payloads into admin workflows so inbound demand is captured, reviewed, and actioned in a single loop.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: I treated the public site and admin as two consumers of one contract, not two products. Next.js owns marketing routing and SEO; the admin stays interaction-heavy and client-driven so operators can manage content, leads, and operations without full-page reloads. That split is what hiring teams look for: the right rendering model per surface, not one SPA for everything.

tradeoffs.considered: Separate CMS for the marketing site
tradeoffs.whyRejected: Would freeze website and admin on different content models and recreate the original disconnect
tradeoffs.whyChosen: Shared API contract and UI patterns across both surfaces

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: I would extract a shared design-system package on day one so tokens, forms, and table patterns never diverge between the public site and the admin.

planora.type: Internal Workflow ERP · RBAC & Real-Time Ops
planora.problem: Internal operations had no system of record for roles, automated modules, and live work state. Handoffs lived in chat and spreadsheets, so permissions were tribal knowledge and no one could see the same operational truth at the same time.
approach: Architected Planora as a full-stack workflow platform: React/Next.js views, FastAPI services, and a permission model that new modules inherit instead of reinventing.
Implemented role-based access control at the module boundary so admins, operators, and viewers only see the workflows they are allowed to run.
Used Cursor AI to scaffold consistent full-stack slices in parallel, then hardened auth, real-time state sync, and shared contracts by hand.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: Planora had to ship many operational modules in parallel without turning into a permission snowflake per screen. I used Cursor AI to scaffold consistent slices — React views, FastAPI endpoints, permission checks — then locked a shared auth and state layer by hand. Guards live at the module boundary so a new workflow inherits access rules. That is the difference between a dashboard and an internal product.

tradeoffs.whyRejected: Could not match internal role models or real-time operational state without heavy customization cost
tradeoffs.whyChosen: Custom React + FastAPI platform with prompt-driven module scaffolding and a shared RBAC contract

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: I would introduce a typed event bus earlier so real-time updates and audit history share one contract instead of per-module sockets.

time4digital.problem: A Luxembourg agency needed six-plus client sites shipped in parallel — architecture, medical transport, retail, and the agency itself. Each brand had to look distinct, stay multilingual (DE/FR/EN), and remain editable by teams who already work in Contao — not wait on a headless rebuild.
approach: Owned build, customization, and deployment of 6+ Contao CMS platforms with reusable layouts, forms, and service catalogs for Luxembourg and German clients.
Shipped TS-Concept (architecture), Luxambulance (emergency medical transport), Modetreff (retail), and Time4Digital’s own presence on one maintainable module kit.
Kept brand-specific CSS and JS on a shared CMS foundation so editors can publish without a new stack per client — the delivery model European agencies actually run.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: Contao was the right CMS because Time4Digital’s editors and LU/DE clients already operate in that stack. Modular layouts, multilingual DE/FR/EN content, and form-heavy service catalogs map to Contao content types, so each brand ships with custom CSS/JS without a headless rebuild. For European hiring managers this is the signal: I can deliver in the CMS the market already uses, not only in a greenfield React app.

tradeoffs.considered: WordPress or a Next.js rebuild per client
tradeoffs.whyRejected: WordPress plugin bloat and weaker editorial structure; a headless rebuild would slow content teams who already know Contao
tradeoffs.whyChosen: Contao CMS with reusable modules and brand-specific styling

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: I would extract a shared Contao module kit and design tokens earlier so spacing, forms, and service grids stay consistent across all six client sites.

terravista.problem: Terra Vista Construction needed a conversion-grade public platform for Arizona luxury homes — services, architectural proof, and consultation booking. A static brochure would leak high-intent visitors before anyone could book a Let’s Talk session.
approach: Built React service modules for custom luxury homes, vacation rentals, tear-down/rebuild, and remodeling, composed so each vertical can iterate without a full-page rewrite.
Shipped architectural portfolio galleries and a Let’s Talk consultation flow at terravistahome.com, designed mobile-first for high-ticket browsing.
Delivered a fully responsive Bootstrap UI across desert, mountain, and woods markets without blocking launch on a listing-index rewrite.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: TerraVista is a marketing-led real estate experience: brand, proof, then booking. React with Bootstrap shipped service modules, galleries, and forms quickly while keeping the visual language stable on mobile. Portfolios and booking stay independent components so either can iterate without a rewrite — velocity with a clean composition boundary, not a monolith page.

tradeoffs.whyRejected: Launch scope was brand, services, and booking — not a large crawlable listing index
tradeoffs.whyChosen: React SPA with Bootstrap for velocity and responsive layout

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: If listing pages grow, I would move the public catalogue to Next.js App Router for SSR and metadata while keeping the booking wizard as a client island.

crayoon.problem: Schools and corporates had no single system for catalogues, size allocation, inventory, and fulfilment. Orders were manual, errors compounded across clients, and stock truth always lagged one spreadsheet behind the warehouse.
approach: Built the operations platform on Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind: catalogues, order flows, and size customizers as reusable modules instead of one-off screens.
Integrated Python FastAPI + PostgreSQL as the source of truth for orders and inventory so the UI never duplicates business rules.
Split the public catalogue (routing and SEO) from a client-side dashboard so state-heavy uniform customizers stay responsive under real operator load.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: Next.js owns routing and SEO on the public catalogue; the internal dashboard stays client-side so state-heavy customizers remain responsive. FastAPI plus PostgreSQL own order and inventory writes so the UI can refetch without duplicating business rules. Server state via React Query plus Context for UI state beat a Redux layer that would have slowed a multi-client ERP cycle.

tradeoffs.whyRejected: Boilerplate overhead for a rapid multi-client delivery cycle
tradeoffs.whyChosen: React Query for server state + Context API for UI state

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: I would have introduced a monorepo earlier to share types between the FastAPI backend and the React frontend so inventory contracts cannot drift.

vigilance.type: Field Security Assessment ERP · Mobile Performance
vigilance.problem: Field managers assessed property security and CCTV on paper, then retyped reports on tablets. Once datasets crossed a few hundred rows, the UI stalled on weak mobile networks — inspections finished in the office, not on site.
approach: Engineered a tablet- and mobile-first inspection app with multi-step forms and dashboards over FastAPI REST APIs.
Applied DOM virtualization and lazy loading so 1,000+ assessment rows stay sortable without extra network round-trips in the field.
Designed dense, touch-first Bootstrap layouts so inspectors complete reports on-site instead of after the visit.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: I chose DOM virtualization over infinite scroll because assessment tables needed consistent sorting across thousands of rows without extra requests on field-strength mobile networks. Infinite scroll would have hidden the sort problem behind pagination. Bootstrap kept the tablet layout dense and touch-friendly without a custom grid. This is a performance problem framed as product: reports that load in the field get filled in the field.

tradeoffs.considered: Standard HTML table rendering every row
tradeoffs.whyChosen: Virtualized list — only visible rows hit the DOM

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: I would add offline-first PWA support so field assessments still work in areas with zero connectivity, then sync when the network returns.

shopq.problem: ShopQ needed a high-conversion public launch surface for a no-code catalog and store platform. Demo booking, pricing, and product proof had to work on every device before the go-to-market window closed — a slow, custom design system would have missed the launch.
approach: Shipped a component-driven React + Bootstrap landing with catalog, pricing, FAQ, and demo-booking flows under a hard GTM deadline.
Implemented Formik + Yup validated lead capture so every demo request is clean enough for sales to act on immediately.
Optimized the conversion path (value → proof → plan → contact) for cross-device reliability instead of delaying launch for a custom token system.

deepDive.architectureReasoning: I chose Bootstrap because the job was conversion under a deadline, not a design-system case study. Pre-built layout and form primitives let me spend time on validated lead capture and the demo-booking path. For GTM landings, shipping a working funnel beats a smaller CSS bundle that arrives after the launch window.

tradeoffs.considered: Custom CSS / design tokens from scratch
tradeoffs.whyRejected: Time-to-market would have slipped the launch window
tradeoffs.whyChosen: Bootstrap utility layer for velocity and consistent responsive behavior

deepDive.wouldDoDifferently: Post-launch I would migrate to Tailwind for tighter design tokens and a smaller CSS bundle, keeping the same conversion architecture.
